title: A Diwali Ticket Home Now Costs Up to Rs 2.5 Lakh From London
excerpt: Fares from the Gulf to Hyderabad are up over 400 percent as workers who skipped trips during months of regional unrest all head home for the festival at once.
body:
• One-way Diwali fares from the Gulf to Hyderabad have surged over 400 percent: Dubai to Hyderabad, usually Rs 13,000 to Rs 39,000, is now priced between Rs 50,000 and Rs 1.5 lakh.
  • A direct London to Hyderabad one-way ticket is costing Rs 2.5 lakh, against a usual Rs 60,000 to Rs 80,000; the cheapest connecting options via Gulf hubs start around Rs 70,000.
  • The return leg is far cheaper — Hyderabad to Gulf cities is available from Rs 12,000 to Rs 24,000 from Monday — so the pain is concentrated on the trip home.
  • Travel agents attribute the spike to festive demand plus pent-up trips: many workers skipped home visits during months of war-related unrest in the region and are all travelling now.

A trip home for Diwali has become the most expensive ticket of the year for Indians working in the Gulf and Europe. One-way fares from the UAE to Hyderabad have risen more than 400 percent, and a direct flight from London is priced at up to Rs 2.5 lakh, The Times of India reported from Hyderabad.

The Numbers, Route by Route

A ticket from Dubai to Hyderabad that usually costs between Rs 13,000 and Rs 39,000 is now priced anywhere between Rs 50,000 and Rs 1.5 lakh. Fares from Abu Dhabi and Sharjah have followed the same pattern, ranging from Rs 45,000 to Rs 1.4 lakh, with Ras Al Khaimah departures also spiking. From London, a direct one-way to Hyderabad costs Rs 2.5 lakh against a usual Rs 60,000 to Rs 80,000, and even connecting flights through Gulf hubs start at around Rs 70,000.

The surge is one-directional. The return journey, from Hyderabad back to the Gulf, is available for as little as Rs 12,000 to Rs 24,000 from Monday — a fraction of the inbound price. The pattern matches the wider UAE-India market: Curly Tales reported fares climbing steeply across UAE-India routes as Diwali nears, with heavy demand for Delhi, Mumbai, Kochi, Bengaluru and Hyderabad.

"A one-way ticket itself is costing more than what we normally spend on a round trip."

— N Karthik, who works in Dubai, to The Times of India

Why This Year Is Worse

Travel agents told the paper the spike combines ordinary festive demand with pent-up travel. Many Indians in the region postponed home visits during the past few months of war-related unrest, and are now trying to make the trip for Diwali at the same time. Moez Meghani of Max Travel noted that working-class Indians employed in the UAE traditionally make a quick dash home for Diwali — short trips of three to five days, unlike the longer winter or Christmas breaks — which concentrates demand into a narrow window around the festival.

What Travellers Can Do With This

The fare pattern itself suggests the options. The return leg is cheap, so the cost sits almost entirely in the days just before Diwali. Connecting itineraries from London start near Rs 70,000 against Rs 2.5 lakh for the direct flight, and shifting the homebound date even a few days changes the fare bucket entirely on routes priced this dynamically. None of that makes the ticket cheap — it makes a Rs 1.5 lakh problem into a smaller one for travellers whose leave dates have any flexibility at all.
